section_summary: This section traces U.S., British, and occupation-authority attention to Japanese broadcasting from January 1945 through April 1946. It covers the apparent effect of Saipan-based American radio, a British request to relay BBC programs in Japan, a proposed NBC-supported commercial network, and SCAP monitoring of Japanese election broadcasts. The section also contains detailed occupation reports on the history, organization, facilities, legal monopoly, and government supervision of the Broadcasting Corporation of Japan.

subfiles.title: Evidence that Saipan Radio Is Successful
subfiles.from: Division of Japanese Affairs; drafted by Kullgren
subfiles.about: Reports that Japan shortened its domestic evening schedule and urged listeners to turn off their radios just before American broadcasts from Saipan began.
subfiles.summary: Memo cites an FCC announcement that Japanese home broadcast schedules changed from January 1 so listeners could retire earlier, and reads the request to switch off sets as evidence Saipan Radio was attracting listeners.

subfiles.title: Letter Forwarding a BBC Rebroadcasting Proposal
subfiles.about: Forwards a British memorandum requesting that selected BBC broadcasts be relayed through Japan's domestic network.
subfiles.summary: Sansom sends Dickover a memorandum on British hopes to rebroadcast BBC programs in Japan, noting uncertainty about British participation in controlling Japanese broadcasting.

subfiles.title: Proposal for Rebroadcasting Certain British Broadcasting Corporation Programmes over the Japanese Domestic Network
subfiles.to: United States authorities and the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Requests SCAP consideration of relaying daily BBC Japanese and English programs over Japan's internal broadcasting network.
subfiles.summary: Memo: Japan's network is under SCAP control but uses local programming; Britain asks that the BBC's daily 1100-1130 GMT service be rebroadcast; the Embassy asks that the Supreme Commander be informed.

subfiles.title: Radio Programs in Japan
subfiles.from: Erle R. Dickover, Department of State
subfiles.about: Records a discussion with Sir George Sansom about how Britain should pursue its BBC rebroadcasting request.
subfiles.summary: Dickover told Sansom SCAP wholly controls Japanese broadcasting, Washington does not set programs, and Radio Tokyo relays no American programs; Britain should approach MacArthur through its Tokyo liaison officer.

subfiles.title: United States Private Company Participation in Proposed Japanese Broadcasting Network
subfiles.from: Harvey B. Otterman, Department of State
subfiles.to: Department of State files; Mr. Turner
subfiles.about: Records NBC's informal inquiry about joining a Japanese syndicate to create a commercial long-wave network.
subfiles.summary: NBC's Frank Russell reported Niles Trammell was approached about a Peoples' Broadcasting Company under Yoshio Miyamoto and sought the Department's informal view; Turner advised no position until MacArthur is consulted.

subfiles.title: Transmitting Preliminary Report on Radio Broadcasting in Japan
subfiles.from: Department of State; drafted by K. Anderson
subfiles.to: Frank A. Schuler Jr., Japan and Korea Branch, OIC
subfiles.about: Transmits a preliminary report on Japanese broadcasting at the War Department's request and asks for confirmation of delivery.
subfiles.summary: Transmittal of a preliminary report on radio broadcasting in Japan requested by the War Department; asks Frank Schuler to confirm receipt.

subfiles.title: DC/R Routing Slip for Despatch No. 372
subfiles.about: Routes Despatch No. 372 among State Department offices and indicates ten copies.
subfiles.summary: Routing slip for Despatch 372 listing offices and ten copies; no substance.

subfiles.title: Periodic SCAP Report: Radio Analysis
subfiles.from: Office of the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards the first SCAP Radio Analysis and explains its purpose, publication schedule, and departmental distribution.
subfiles.summary: Radio Analysis No. 1 from SCAP's Media Analysis Division summarizes the content and trends of Japanese voice broadcasting under occupation supervision, to appear irregularly; six copies sent.

subfiles.title: Radio Analysis No. 1: Special Report on Election Speeches, 14 March–9 April 1946
subfiles.from: Media Analysis Division, Civil Information and Education Section, SCAP
subfiles.to: Office of the United States Political Adviser and Department of State
subfiles.about: Analyzes Japanese political-party and candidate broadcasts during the 1946 general-election campaign.
subfiles.summary: The report surveys 168 party speeches and 810 candidate broadcasts carried through Tokyo, Nagano, Niigata, and Kōfu, providing schedules and numerical breakdowns by district. It summarizes the platforms of the Liberal, Progressive, Socialist, Communist, Cooperative, and Rikken Yosei parties on the emperor system, constitutional reform, food, land, labor, inflation, production, and women's suffrage. The analysis contrasts conservative emperor-centered positions with socialist and communist programs and closes with a long list of participating parties and political groups.

subfiles.title: Reports on Japanese Radio Broadcasting
subfiles.from: Office of the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits SCAP reports on the history, supervision, charter, organization, and leading personnel of Japanese broadcasting.
subfiles.summary: Despatch sends reports on the history of the Japanese radio industry, broadcast supervision and the Broadcasting Corporation's charter, with biographical notes on officials.

subfiles.title: History of the Japanese Radio Industry
subfiles.from: Radio Research Unit, Civil Information and Education Section, SCAP
subfiles.about: Surveys the development, organization, programming, overseas expansion, networks, subscribers, and receiver supply of Japanese broadcasting from 1923 to 1946.
subfiles.summary: The report traces broadcasting from the 1923 private-broadcasting regulations and the early Tokyo, Nagoya, and Osaka bureaus through creation of the nationwide Broadcasting Corporation of Japan. It describes the expansion of central and local stations, relay networks, program-planning bodies, colonial and overseas links, and wartime government control. It also outlines the three postwar networks—including the Armed Forces Radio Service network—and evaluates subscriber totals, wartime losses, and the uncertain number of usable receivers.

subfiles.title: Supervision of the Broadcasting Industry
subfiles.from: Radio Research Unit, Civil Information and Education Section, SCAP
subfiles.about: Translates a 1932 account of the legal basis and administrative mechanisms for government control of Japanese broadcasting.
subfiles.summary: The report explains why broadcasting was entrusted to a single nonprofit juridical corporation even though wireless telephone was legally subject to state supervision. It describes the Broadcasting Corporation of Japan's monopoly status and its triple supervision as a nonprofit body, special industry, and operator of wireless facilities. Detailed sections enumerate ministerial authority over corporate officers, meetings, budgets, construction, station personnel, schedules, subscriber fees, program filing, advertising, censorship, inspections, and penalties.
